# Crawler Robustness Gap Analysis: What Commercial Platforms Handle That We Don't

**Prepared:** 2026-07-24
**Type:** Desk research / gap analysis (no live URL corpus — findings drawn entirely from vendor documentation, changelogs, pricing pages, and reference-project source/docs, each cited).

## Scope

Our crawler currently handles 21 edge cases:

**Original 17:** (1) JS render, (2) DNS failure, (3) Timeout, (4) Pagination, (5) Rate limit / IP ban, (6) Heavy antibot (Cloudflare/Akamai/DataDome/PerimeterX/Imperva/Kasada), (7) Simple image-text captcha, (8) reCAPTCHA v2/v3/enterprise, (9) hCaptcha, (10) Lazy loading, (11) Calendar infinite loop, (12) Homepage/redirect loop, (13) Other loops, (14) Infinite scroll, (15) SSL/cert/connection error, (16) GeoIP block, (17) Auth/login wall (detect & skip).

**Already added 4:** Paywall, consent/cookie wall, soft 404, faceted-URL explosion.

This document covers **only cases missing from that list of 21**, found by researching 13 commercial crawling/scraping vendors (Firecrawl, Zyte, Bright Data, Apify/Crawlee, ScrapingBee, ScraperAPI, Oxylabs, Crawlbase, Diffbot, Octoparse, Import.io, ScrapingAnt, SerpApi) and 6 open-source/standards references (Scrapy, Apache Nutch, StormCrawler, Heritrix, Common Crawl, Google Search Central).

## Methodology & confidence notes

- Every claim below comes from a page an agent directly fetched and read (WebFetch), not a search-result snippet, unless explicitly marked otherwise.
- Where a lead looked promising in a search snippet but **failed re-verification** on the actual page, it is noted as a failed lead rather than silently dropped or silently included — see the "Marketing vs. documentation" section.
- **Import.io** is mid-acquisition (acquired by Neuralogics, announced Oct 2025) and its own docs site currently reads "Sorry, it's a bit messy here but worry not! We are currently revamping our docs" — treat Import.io findings as lower-confidence than the rest.
- Three vendors (Oxylabs Web Scraper API, Crawlbase Crawling API, ScrapingAnt) are architecturally "fetch/render one URL I give you" APIs, not autonomous spiders — this is *why* they have no robots.txt/sitemap/canonical-dedup documentation at all: it's out of scope for the product shape, not an oversight. Diffbot, Apify, and the open-source crawlers are true autonomous spiders and are the richest sources for frontier-management edge cases accordingly.

---

## 1. Missing Edge Cases

| Edge case | Vendors/tools that call it out | Why it breaks a naive crawler | How hard to detect | How hard to fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **robots.txt & crawl-delay compliance** | Diffbot, Bright Data, Firecrawl, StormCrawler, Common Crawl, Google Search Central, Apache Nutch, Crawlee, Apify | Naive crawlers hit explicitly-excluded paths (admin, search trees, calendar generators), triggering bans or legal exposure, and ignore `Crawl-delay`, hammering slow servers into blocking them. | **Trivial** — one `GET /robots.txt` per host, cached with a TTL. | **Easy** — parse with a maintained library (`protego`/`reppy` in Python, crawler-commons in Java); gate frontier + delay accordingly. |
| **Sitemap discovery (sitemap.xml / sitemap-index / gzip)** | Diffbot, Crawlee, StormCrawler, Apache Nutch, Common Crawl, Firecrawl | Without sitemap seeding a crawler must discover every URL by following links, missing orphan pages with no inlinks and wasting budget rediscovering structure the site already published; gzipped/indexed sitemaps are silently skipped if only plain XML is handled. | **Easy** — check robots.txt `Sitemap:` directive, else probe `/sitemap.xml`, `/sitemap_index.xml`. | **Easy** — stdlib XML parsing + gzip decompression + recurse into `<sitemapindex>` entries. |
| **Canonical tag + duplicate/near-duplicate content consolidation** | Diffbot (strongest: 3 distinct mechanisms), Google Search Central (signal-strength hierarchy), Apify, Apache Nutch (near-dup via token-frequency signature), Firecrawl (confirmed gap: URL-string dedup only, no canonical-tag reading), Zyte (canonical surfaced as data field only, not active dedup) | Template-driven sites serve the same content under many URLs (session params, sort orders, print views); without canonical resolution the crawler stores N copies of one document and burns N× the budget — directly extends the faceted-URL-explosion case we already handle. | **Easy** — parse `<link rel="canonical" href="...">`; true near-dup detection needs content hashing. | **Medium** — exact dedup (hash + keep one) is easy; near-duplicate tolerance (Nutch's token-frequency fingerprint style) is a real feature-build. |
| **Charset/encoding detection (non-UTF-8, mojibake)** | Zyte (names the WHATWG HTML5 sniffing algorithm), StormCrawler, Apache Nutch, Common Crawl errata, Firecrawl (weak, 1-line changelog) | Pages served without a correct charset header (common on older/regional government and enterprise sites) get decoded as UTF-8/Latin-1 by default, producing mojibake that corrupts every downstream text field. | **Easy** — read `charset=` from Content-Type; if absent/wrong, byte-sniff. | **Easy** — `charset-normalizer`/`chardet` (Python) or ICU4J (Java) as fallback; cap sniffing to first ~10KB for speed (StormCrawler's pattern). |
| **Non-HTML content types (PDF/DOC/XLS/ZIP) — detection & routing** | Firecrawl (OCR fallback engine), Diffbot (PDF via Extract/Bulk, candidly variable quality), Octoparse, Apache Nutch (Tika integration), Oxylabs (confirmed gap: images only, no PDF/DOC/XLS found) | A crawler that always tries an HTML parser on the response body will crash or silently save garbage binary as "text" when the response is actually a PDF/DOC/XLS/ZIP — very common for report/notice/form attachments. | **Trivial** — check Content-Type AND sniff magic bytes (`%PDF-`, `PK\x03\x04`), since Content-Type is frequently wrong or missing. | **Medium** — routing/skipping is cheap; actual text extraction (pdfminer/PyMuPDF/Tika) is a real, non-trivial build; OCR fallback is a bigger lift still. |
| **Huge-file / tarpit defense** | Zyte (10MB/500MB caps), Scrapy (`DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE`=1GiB, `DOWNLOAD_WARNSIZE`=32MiB), Apify (1-hour download timeout + min-speed abort), ScraperAPI (50MB cap) | A malicious or misconfigured endpoint can stream gigabytes down a connection the crawler assumed was a normal HTML page, hanging a worker or exhausting memory/disk. | **Trivial** — check `Content-Length` before download; cap bytes read while streaming if absent. | **Easy** — hard byte ceiling + abort, plus a minimum-throughput timeout to catch slow-drip tarpits. |
| **Compression bombs** (decompression-side, distinct from raw huge-file) | Zyte (auto-decompress then apply cap **post**-decompression — explicit zip-bomb guard), Scrapy (`HttpCompressionMiddleware` handles gzip/deflate/brotli/zstd) | A small compressed payload (KBs) can decompress into gigabytes in memory — a classic decompression-bomb DoS a wire-level size check won't catch. | **Medium** — must inspect size *after* decompression, streaming. | **Easy once recognized** — decompress into a bounded buffer, abort mid-stream the instant the cap is exceeded. |
| **Meta-refresh & JS redirects** | Scrapy (`MetaRefreshMiddleware`, `METAREFRESH_MAXDELAY`=100s), Diffbot (follows meta-refresh, exposes `resolvedPageUrl`, documents a pattern-matching gotcha), Zyte (implied via "other URL changes" during render) | Legacy/gov/enterprise sites often redirect via `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` instead of an HTTP 3xx; a crawler that only follows `Location` headers stores the empty stub and never reaches real content. | **Easy** — regex for `http-equiv=["']refresh["']` in the fetched body. | **Easy** — parse the `content` attribute's `url=` fragment and re-queue; no browser needed unless the destination is itself JS-computed. |
| **SPA history-API routing & hash-based routes** | Bright Data (`x-unblock-url-fragment` header), Diffbot (explicitly does **not** follow `#`-fragment links — documented limitation), Google Search Central (explicitly rejects hash-fragment crawling, prescribes History API) | URL fragments never reach the server by HTTP definition; a crawler treating `/page#/foo` and `/page#/bar` as distinct either creates false duplicates or (more commonly) never visits the JS-rendered content behind hash routes at all. | **Medium** — needs a real browser or a manual route map; not cheaply detectable from headers alone. | **Hard** for true SPA hash-routing (needs a browser); cheap partial fix is recognizing and logging `#!`/hashbang patterns instead of silently discarding them. |
| **hreflang/i18n URL multiplication** | Google Search Central only — confirmed **absent** from every one of the 13 commercial vendors researched | Sites publishing 20–40 language/region variants via `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="...">` can multiply one logical document into dozens of crawlable URLs; without consolidation the crawler treats every locale as unique content. | **Easy** — parse `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="...">` tags. | **Medium** — Google's bidirectional-confirmation rule (a hreflang link only counts if reciprocated) is a cheap heuristic to borrow; full cross-language content-equivalence checking needs more than regex. |
| **Iframe content extraction** | ScrapingAnt (dedicated `iframes` JSON field), Zyte (`includeIframes` param), Bright Data (frame access is a debug tool only, not extraction) | Content embedded via `<iframe>` (maps, payment widgets, some document viewers) lives in a document the parent page's DOM never contains; parsing only the outer HTML misses it entirely. | **Easy** — flag `<iframe src="...">` and queue the `src` as a child fetch. | **Medium** — same-origin iframes are a straightforward child-fetch-and-merge; cross-origin iframes needing their own JS execution require a real browser. |
| **Shadow DOM content extraction** | **No vendor solves this** — Zyte's own docs explicitly state selectors "cannot interact with... the shadow DOM"; Bright Data and Firecrawl never mention it at all | Web components deliberately encapsulate markup inside a shadow root to isolate it from outside DOM queries — by design, regular HTML parsing can't see inside it, and this is confirmed unsolved industry-wide, not just a gap in our list. | **Hard** — requires a real browser walking `element.shadowRoot` recursively; raw HTML source never contains shadow content at all. | **Hard** — a CDP/Playwright script that walks shadow roots is the only known approach; no vendor has shipped and documented this. |
| **HTTP/2-or-3-only hosts** | Common Crawl (explicit dual-stack HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2-over-TLS support), Oxylabs (HTTP/3 for its Residential/Mobile Proxies only, not the Scraper API product), Bright Data (bare 3-word mention) | A growing number of hosts (edge/QUIC-only deployments, some behind Cloudflare) negotiate exclusively via HTTP/2 or HTTP/3; an HTTP/1.1-only client gets a connection failure indistinguishable from "host is down." | **Medium** — needs a client that reports negotiated ALPN protocol/failure reason distinctly from a generic timeout. | **Medium** — swap to an HTTP/2-and-3-capable client stack (e.g. `httpx`/`hyper`); an infrastructure change, not a config flag. |
| **Cookie/session bootstrap requirements** | Zyte, Bright Data, Crawlbase, Oxylabs, ScraperAPI, ScrapingBee, Crawlee — the single most cross-vendor-consistent finding in this entire research pass | Many sites (WAF'd, geofenced, A/B-cookied) return a warm-up `Set-Cookie` on the first hit and soft-block a second request that doesn't echo it; a stateless crawler looks like a brand-new visitor every request and gets challenged repeatedly. | **Medium** — compare status/content-length of a stateless 2nd request vs. one replaying 1st-response cookies; divergence signals a bootstrap requirement. | **Easy** — a persistent cookie jar / session object per host (a one-line change in most HTTP libraries) instead of independent stateless requests. |
| **POST-only or GraphQL-backed content** | Oxylabs, Bright Data, ScraperAPI, ScrapingAnt (all: raw POST body passthrough), Apify Academy (GraphQL detection heuristic: POST to a `/graphql`-suffixed endpoint is "99.99% bulletproof") | Content-heavy modern sites (search results, filtered listings, infinite-scroll feeds) are frequently rendered from a POST-based internal API or a single GraphQL endpoint — a GET-only crawler never sees this content regardless of how well it handles everything else. | **Medium** — network-capture during a real browser render (recording XHR/fetch) is the only reliable discovery method; static HTML gives no hint these endpoints exist. | **Hard** for novel APIs (reverse-engineering the schema); **easy** once the schema is known (replay the same query with pagination cursors swapped). |
| **WAF soft-blocks returning HTTP 200** | Weakest-substantiated finding across the *entire* research pass — Bright Data's "Data Integrity Validations" discloses no mechanism; Zyte defines "ban" status-code-agnostically but never claims 200-body classification; Crawlbase's `custom_success_codes` is the *inverse* problem; Apify Academy names the category ("deceptive responses") without a detector; technique borrowed from Google's soft-404 doc (content-based, not status-based) | A WAF/bot-mitigation product often returns a normal 200 with a page that says "Access Denied" or is a near-empty shell; a pipeline that treats "200 = success" silently stores block-pages as real content — worse than an honest failure because nothing downstream flags it. | **Medium** — a heuristic combination (body length far below that host's historical median, known block-page keywords/title patterns) catches most cases; no vendor documents anything stronger. | **Medium** — once flagged, retry via an escalated tier (proxy rotation, JS-challenge solve, real browser) rather than accepting the response. |
| **Stale-content / change-detection & revisit policy** | Firecrawl (`changeStatus` new/same/changed/removed, git-diff + JSON diff modes), Apache Nutch (`AdaptiveFetchSchedule`: `inc_rate`=0.4/`dec_rate`=0.2 per-URL interval adjustment), Common Crawl (adaptive recrawl built on Nutch's CrawlDB), Diffbot (round-based, not cron-based, recurring schedule), Crawlbase (honestly documents **no** change detection — just overwrite-on-recrawl), Google Search Central ("staleness" as 1 of 3 crawl-demand signals) | A fixed recrawl schedule either wastes budget re-fetching pages that never change, or misses updates on fast-changing pages; for time-sensitive content (notices, reports, listings), "when did this change" matters as much as "what does it say now." | **Easy-Medium** — a content hash compared run-over-run tells you changed-y/n cheaply; classifying *how* it changed is more work. | **Medium** — Nutch's `AdaptiveFetchSchedule` formula (shrink interval on change, grow on no-change, bounded min/max) is a well-documented, directly portable algorithm. |
| **Malformed HTML recovery** | Weak/absent almost everywhere — a Zyte lead was explicitly chased and **failed** re-verification; the one concrete finding is Apache Nutch's pluggable `parser.html.impl` (neko/tagsoup, both tolerant by design); ScrapingAnt's AI extractor sidesteps the problem by only ever operating on converted Markdown, never raw HTML | Real-world HTML (especially from older CMSes) routinely violates spec — unclosed tags, invalid nesting; a strict parser throws or silently truncates the DOM at the first malformed tag. | **Easy** — most strict parsers raise a distinct exception on malformed markup. | **Trivial** — swap to a lenient/tag-soup-tolerant parser (`lxml` recover mode, `html5lib`); likely the single cheapest fix in this whole table, probably why almost nobody bothers advertising it as a "feature." |
| **Very deep DOM / huge pages (OOM)** | Scrapy (`MEMUSAGE_LIMIT_MB`, `SCRAPER_SLOT_MAX_ACTIVE_SIZE`=5MB soft cap, explicit BFO-over-DFO recommendation "to save memory"), Firecrawl (self-host CPU/RAM reject-threshold, default 0.8) | An extremely large single page (an unpaginated "load more" listing, a giant data table) can blow past available memory during DOM parsing alone, independent of any network-level size cap, taking down the whole worker. | **Medium** — track parse-time memory delta per page, or pre-check byte size against a DOM-parse-safe ceiling. | **Medium** — cap the parser's own memory/node-count budget; prefer streaming/SAX-style parsing above a size threshold. |
| **Server-side A/B or personalized variants** | **None found** — confirmed absent across all 13 commercial vendors and all 6 reference sources | Some sites serve structurally different HTML to different visitors (A/B tests, personalization) for the identical URL; re-crawling the same URL twice can produce two different, both-valid-looking documents. The industry appears to treat this as fully out of scope. | **Hard** — requires either multiple fetches of the same URL compared for divergence, or vendor cooperation. | **Hard** — no clean fix exists anywhere in the industry; at best, flag URLs whose hash changes between same-day refetches as "unstable." |
| **Mobile-vs-desktop User-Agent divergence** | Zyte (full header-set profiles, not just a UA string), Bright Data (CDP device emulation, "hundreds of real devices"), Oxylabs (12 distinct `user_agent_type` values), SerpApi (device param with a defined device fleet), Diffbot (UA array rotation) | Many sites (especially older responsive breakpoints on government/procurement portals) serve a meaningfully different DOM, or different content, to mobile vs. desktop UAs; a crawler that never varies its UA can silently miss a content variant. | **Trivial** — nothing to detect; this is a deliberate config choice, not a failure mode. | **Trivial** — pick one UA string deliberately and stay consistent within a crawl, instead of leaving it to whatever the HTTP client defaults to. |
| **Generic structural crawl-trap bounds** (URL length, path-segment repetition, hop-count budget) | Scrapy (`URLLENGTH_LIMIT`=2083, "prevent infinite-length URL attacks"), Heritrix (`PathologicalPathDecideRule`, `TooManyPathSegmentsDecideRule`, `TooManyHopsDecideRule` default max=20 — the canonical reference implementation), StormCrawler (`BasicURLFilter` — length + path-element repetition), Apache Nutch (repeating-path-segment regex, `db.max.outlink.length`=4096) | Our baseline targets specific *known* trap shapes (calendars, redirect loops); this is the generic, pattern-agnostic safety net that catches trap shapes we haven't seen yet, without needing to recognize the specific pattern first. | **Trivial** — pure string operations, zero network cost, evaluated before a URL is even queued. | **Trivial** — reject/dedupe at enqueue time; closer to "add a guard clause" than "build a feature." |
| **Adaptive/self-tuning crawl-rate throttling** (proactive, not reactive) | Scrapy AutoThrottle (`target_delay = latency / AUTOTHROTTLE_TARGET_CONCURRENCY`; non-200 responses only ever *increase* delay), Heritrix (`delay-factor`/`min-interval-ms`), Common Crawl (adaptive back-off specifically on 429/5xx), Zyte (worked concurrency-from-RPM formula) | Our baseline's rate-limit handling is reactive (respond once banned); this is the proactive complement — measuring real server latency and self-adjusting delay *before* triggering a ban, avoiding burned IPs/proxy budget on avoidable bans. | N/A — a policy to implement, not a failure to detect. | **Easy** — Scrapy's published formula is directly portable to any crawler. |
| **Honeypot trap links** (invisible bait links/fields) | Octoparse ("a honeypot is a trap...invisible to humans but visible to scrapers"; defended via precise XPath/selector targeting) | Some sites deliberately hide links/fields via CSS purely to catch crawlers that follow every `<a>` or fill every `<input>`; a human never sees them, but a naive crawler does, immediately flagging itself as a bot. | **Medium** — requires checking computed CSS visibility (display/visibility/size/position), not just DOM presence. | **Easy once detected** — exclude links/fields matching common hide patterns from the follow/fill set. |
| **AI/TDM scraping-consent signals** (TDMRep, ai.txt — a layer beyond robots.txt) | ScrapingBee blog — the only source that surfaced this at all, in unusual technical depth | A newer, separate consent layer for AI/text-and-data-mining use: `/.well-known/tdmrep.json`, an HTTP `tdm-reservation` header, or `<meta name="tdm-reservation">` (precedence: meta > header > well-known file), plus a robots.txt-styled `/ai.txt` that — unlike robots.txt — defaults to **opted-out** if no file is served at all. Directly relevant: EU AI Act Article 53 GPAI obligations take effect 2 August 2026, nine days after this report's date. | **Easy** — three fixed, well-known locations to check. | **Easy** to detect/log; *acting* on an opt-out signal found is a governance decision, not an engineering one. |
| **Mutual-TLS / client-certificate-gated sites** | Bright Data (CDP `Browser.addCertificate` — session-scoped client cert for sites requiring the *client*, not just the target, to present one) | Distinct from our baseline's SSL/cert error (handling the *target's* broken cert): some gov/enterprise sites require the *crawler* to present a valid client cert before completing the TLS handshake; the failure looks identical to a generic SSL error but has a completely different fix. | **Medium** — a mutual-TLS handshake failure has a distinct TLS alert code, but most HTTP libraries don't surface it distinctly by default. | **Hard** — requires acquiring and provisioning an actual client certificate, an out-of-band/often-manual process. |
| **Self-healing / automatic scraper-breakage detection** | Crawlbase (error 425: "Page structure changed and the scraper couldn't extract data. Reported automatically") | Distinct from stale-*content* detection above — this detects that the *extraction logic* broke because a site's template changed, not that the underlying data changed; hardcoded selectors silently return empty/wrong fields forever after a redesign otherwise. | **Medium** — compare the shape of extracted output (field count/presence) against a historical per-template baseline; a sudden drop signals breakage. | **Hard** — automatic re-mapping (what Import.io vaguely markets as "self-healing" with zero disclosed mechanism) is a real ML/heuristic problem; a cheap partial fix is alerting a human when field-presence drops. |
| **Dark-web (.onion) routing** | Crawlbase (`tor_network` boolean parameter) | Niche: `.onion` targets are unreachable without Tor-circuit routing; a standard crawler gets a DNS failure indistinguishable from a typo'd domain. | **Trivial** — `.onion` TLD is a simple string match. | **Medium** — requires a Tor client/proxy in the fetch path, an infrastructure dependency. |
| **Malicious-URL / threat-protection blocklisting** | Firecrawl (checks target URLs against Google Web Risk classifier pre-fetch, configurable risk threshold) | Protects the *crawler*, not the data — a broad or referral-driven crawl can be redirected toward malware/phishing hosts; fetching them risks pulling exploit payloads into crawling infrastructure. | **Easy** — Web Risk / Safe Browsing lookup is a simple pre-fetch API call, cacheable per domain. | **Easy** — reject/skip before fetch if flagged; no browser needed. |

## 2. Ranked Top 10 — Impact × Ease of Cheap Detection

Ranked by (impact on a real crawl) × (ease of adding a **non-browser** detector — header/regex/heuristic only).

1. **robots.txt & crawl-delay compliance** — *Cheapest detector:* one `GET /robots.txt` per host (cache with TTL), parsed by an off-the-shelf library (`protego`/`reppy`); gate every new host's frontier + delay on it before the first real fetch.
2. **Canonical tag consolidation** — *Cheapest detector:* regex `rel=["']canonical["'][^>]+href=["']([^"']+)["']` against the fetched `<head>`; directly shrinks the faceted/duplicate-URL explosion we already partially handle.
3. **Generic structural crawl-trap bounds** — *Cheapest detector:* reject any URL over ~2000 chars, or where a path segment repeats 3+ times (`re.search(r'(/[^/]+)\1{2,}', path)`) — zero network cost, catches trap shapes we haven't pattern-matched yet.
4. **Sitemap.xml / sitemap-index / gzip discovery** — *Cheapest detector:* check the robots.txt `Sitemap:` line, else probe `/sitemap.xml` and `/sitemap_index.xml`; gunzip + recurse `<sitemapindex>` with stdlib only.
5. **Non-HTML content-type detection & safe routing** — *Cheapest detector:* check `Content-Type` header **and** sniff the first 4 bytes (`%PDF`, `PK\x03\x04`) before handing the body to an HTML parser — prevents crashes/corrupted saves on every PDF/DOC/XLS attachment.
6. **Huge-file / tarpit defense** — *Cheapest detector:* check `Content-Length` pre-download; while streaming, abort past a byte ceiling (Scrapy's 1GiB default is a reasonable start) and separately abort on sub-floor throughput.
7. **Charset/mojibake detection** — *Cheapest detector:* read `charset=` from `Content-Type`; on absence or decode failure, fall back to `charset-normalizer`/`chardet`, capped to the first ~10KB for speed.
8. **Meta-refresh / JS-redirect stub detection** — *Cheapest detector:* regex for `http-equiv=["']refresh["']` in the fetched body, extract the `url=` fragment, re-queue.
9. **WAF soft-block-as-200 heuristic** — *Cheapest detector:* flag any 200 whose body length is a statistical outlier vs. that host's running median, or whose title/body hits a short block-page keyword list ("access denied", "attention required", "verify you are human", "just a moment"). No vendor documents anything cheaper or more reliable.
10. **Cookie/session bootstrap detection** — *Cheapest detector:* per new host, issue one cookie-less request and one replaying the first response's `Set-Cookie`; if status/length diverge, switch that host to a persistent session object for the rest of the crawl.

**Honorable mention (#11, arguably the single cheapest fix in the whole analysis but lower-frequency impact):** malformed HTML recovery — swap the parser to a lenient/tag-soup-tolerant mode (`lxml` recover, `html5lib`); essentially a one-line change, which is probably why almost no vendor bothers to advertise it as a feature.

| Octoparse | Residential proxy / CAPTCHA add-ons | $3/GB and $1–1.5/1000 respectively, on top of tier cost | octoparse.com/pricing |
| SerpApi | Zero-retention mode ("ZeroTrace") | Oddly gated to **Free and Enterprise tiers only** — absent from every mid-tier | serpapi.com/pricing |
| SerpApi | Request throughput | Hourly caps scale by tier: 50/hr (Free) up to 6,000/hr ($275/mo Big Data) | serpapi.com/pricing |

**Pattern across vendors:** JS/browser rendering, residential/mobile proxy IPs, precise sub-country geotargeting, robots.txt bypass, and CAPTCHA-solving are the five features most consistently metered or tier-gated. Plain HTTP fetching of ordinary pages is cheap or free everywhere; everything that helps evade detection or targeting costs materially more.

---

## 4. Industry-Wide Gaps (not just gaps in our list — nobody has solved these)

- **Shadow DOM content extraction** — zero vendors researched can reach it; Zyte is the only one honest enough to say so explicitly.
- **hreflang/i18n URL consolidation** — only Google Search Central documents a mechanism (bidirectional-confirmation); not one of 13 commercial vendors addresses it.
- **Server-side A/B / personalization normalization** — no evidence from any of the 19 sources researched.
- **Malformed HTML recovery as a named, verified feature** — every vendor lead either wasn't found or, in Zyte's case, was explicitly chased down and failed re-verification. The only real evidence is Apache Nutch's parser choice (neko/tagsoup).
- **WAF soft-block-as-200 detection** — every vendor examined is vague-to-silent on this specific mechanism, despite several vendors (Bright Data, Zyte) clearly caring about ban detection generally. This is a genuine, currently-unfilled niche in commercial tooling, not just in our crawler.

---

## 5. Marketing vs. Documentation — Flagged Discrepancies

Per the request to be skeptical, these are specific instances where a vendor's marketing claim did not survive being checked against its own technical documentation:

- **Zyte pricing page vs. Zyte API docs:** the pricing page (zyte.com/pricing) claims "No feature restrictions, no hidden limitations" and "Large downloads (up to 100MB)" — directly contradicted by docs.zyte.com's own **10MB** truncation limit and its own metered add-on list (screenshots, extraction, custom attributes, residential IP/geo surcharges).
- **ScrapingAnt's "CAPTCHA and Cloudflare" doc page** (docs.scrapingant.com/captcha-and-cloudflare) is titled as a technical explainer but on direct read contains no actual CAPTCHA-solving or Cloudflare-challenge-specific mechanism — only generic "real browser" fingerprint-realism language.
- **Import.io's "self-healing" claim** (import.io/products): "our extractors don't break. They adapt in real-time, using machine learning to re-map layouts" — no algorithm, detection method, or fallback behavior disclosed anywhere.
- **SerpApi's "U.S. Legal Shield"** — listed as a named feature on every single pricing tier (serpapi.com/pricing) with zero explanatory text found anywhere on the site.
- **SerpApi's CAPTCHA-solving blog post** (serpapi.com/blog/captchas-and-captcha-solving/) claims "reliable, CAPTCHA-solving mechanisms" with no CAPTCHA type, automation approach, or retry logic disclosed — marketing copy on a page titled as a technical explainer.
- **Bright Data's "Data Integrity Validations"** (brightdata.com/products/web-unlocker) — described only as validating via "request timing, data types, and response content," no algorithm or signature named.
- **Firecrawl's "sitemap poisoning" fix** (changelog, Apr 2025 v1.7.0) — claimed fixed, but direct inspection of the public `sitemap.ts` source found no visible URL-count cap, byte cap, or recursion-depth counter to substantiate the claim.
- **Bright Data's own internal inconsistency:** Scraping Browser max session duration is documented as **60 minutes** on two docs.brightdata.com pages but **30 minutes** on Bright Data's own GitHub reference doc.
- **A Zyte "HTML5-spec normalization" claim** (malformed-HTML recovery) appeared in search results but was explicitly chased down against docs.zyte.com's `browser.html` and `reference.html` pages and found unsubstantiated — flagged as a failed lead, not included as evidence anywhere above.
